```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(emss)
library(ggplot2)
options(width = 90, digits = 4)
```

This article explains what `emss` computes and why. It works through a
12-item example by hand, checks every hand calculation against `emss`, and
then states the mathematical properties of the two criteria, ESS-Count and
ESS-Weight, with short proofs. For day-to-day use of the package, start with
[Getting started](getting-started.html). [Manual cut
scores](manual-cut-scores.html), the [bootstrap](bootstrapping.html), and [Item Location](item-locations.html) have
their own articles.

# The idea

In **embedded standard setting** (ESS; Lewis & Cook, 2020), content experts
align each test item to the performance level descriptor (PLD), also called
the achievement level descriptor (ALD), whose knowledge and skills the item
calls for. The alignment is part of item development rather than a separate
standard-setting meeting, so the performance standards are *embedded* in the
test's design. ESS has been used in K-12 assessment and in credentialing
(Lewis, Graw, & Baker, 2024).

Each item also has a **location** on the reporting scale, typically a
response-probability location such as RP67: the scale score at which an
examinee has a 67% chance of answering the item correctly. When the
descriptors and the scale tell the same story, items aligned to higher
levels sit higher on the scale. A cut score for a level is then placed where
the order of the items on the scale agrees best with their aligned levels:

* items aligned **at or above** the level should be located **at or above**
  its cut score, and
* items aligned **below** the level should be located **below** it.

An item on the wrong side of a cut is **inconsistent** with that cut. ESS
places every cut where inconsistency is smallest. The two versions differ
only in how they measure it:

* **ESS-Count** counts the inconsistent items (i.e., where matters, not how far).
* **ESS-Weight** adds up how far the inconsistent items are from the cut on
  the location scale (i.e., how far matters, not where).

Lewis, Lee and Choi (2021) compared the two algorithms.

# Notation

The analysis is carried out separately for each **unit**: one grade, one
rating round and one item subset (all items, or one content domain; see
[Analysis units](#sec-units)). Within a unit:

| Symbol | Meaning |
|:--|:--|
| $n$ | number of items |
| $b_i$ | location of item $i$ (the column named by `location`, such as RP67) |
| $b_{(1)} \le \dots \le b_{(n)}$ | locations in increasing order; the position $p$ of an item in this order is its **page** in the ordered item booklet |
| $K$ | number of performance levels, ordered $1 < 2 < \dots < K$ |
| $a_{ij}$ | level panelist $j$ aligned item $i$ to ($j = 1, \dots, J$) |
| $a_i$ | the item's aligned level used for the cut (one panelist's $a_{ij}$, or the modal level across panelists) |
| $k$ | a cut level, $k = 2, \dots, K$: the cut $c_k$ is the lowest score in level $k$ |
| $U_k = \{i : a_i \ge k\}$ | items aligned at or above level $k$ ("upper" items) |
| $L_k = \{i : a_i < k\}$ | items aligned below level $k$ ("lower" items); $n_{<k} = \lvert L_k \rvert$ |
| $\sigma$ | the grade's SD; weights are divided by it (default 1) |
| $o_i$ | empirical level of item $i$, implied by the cut scores |

Items with the same location are ordered by `Order_of_Difficulty` and then by
input order. This affects only the page numbers shown, not the cut scores.

# A worked example

Twelve items in grade "G5" have RP67 locations between 212 and 297. Three
panelists aligned each item to one of three levels: Basic, Proficient and
Advanced.

```{r}
#| label: toy-data
items <- data.frame(
  Grade   = "G5",
  Item_ID = c(paste0("I0", 1:9), paste0("I", 10:12)),
  RP67    = c(212, 224, 231, 239, 246, 252, 258, 265, 271, 280, 288, 297)
)
labels <- c("Basic", "Proficient", "Advanced")
alignments <- list(                       # 1 = Basic, 2 = Proficient, 3 = Advanced
  P1 = c(1, 1, 2, 2, 1, 2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 3),
  P2 = c(1, 1, 1, 2, 1, 1, 2, 3, 3, 2, 3, 3),
  P3 = c(1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 1, 2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3)
)
ratings <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(alignments), function(p) data.frame(
  Grade = "G5", Table = "T1", Panelist = p, Item_ID = items$Item_ID,
  ALD = labels[alignments[[p]]])))
head(ratings, 3)
```

A small score distribution provides impact data:

```{r}
#| label: toy-examinees
scores <- data.frame(Grade = "G5", Score = seq(200, 310, by = 5))
scores$Freq <- round(400 * dnorm(scores$Score, mean = 255, sd = 25))
```

`ess_data()` combines the inputs, and `emstans()` runs both criteria:

```{r}
#| label: toy-fit
d <- ess_data(ratings, items, examinees = scores, levels = labels)
res_w <- emstans(data = d, location = "RP67", method = "weight")
res_c <- emstans(data = d, location = "RP67", method = "count")
res_w
res_c
```

The two criteria agree on the Advanced cut and disagree on the Proficient
cut. The rest of this article shows where every one of these numbers comes
from.

# Step 1: one aligned level per item

Cut scores are estimated for each panelist's own alignments and for the
**modal** alignment across panelists. The modal level of item $i$ is the
level chosen by the most panelists:

$$
a_i = \operatorname*{arg\,max}_{\ell} \; \#\{\, j : a_{ij} = \ell \,\}.
$$

When two or more levels tie for most votes, the tie goes to the level chosen
by the panelist whose alignments agree best with the item locations,
measured by the Pearson correlation across the unit's items:

$$
r_j = \operatorname{cor}\big( (a_{1j}, \dots, a_{nj}),\; (b_1, \dots, b_n) \big).
$$

If panelists have equal correlations, the one whose ID comes first in sorted
order wins. Modal levels are computed for each table and for all tables
together. The all-tables modal result is the one used for agreement, the
item review and impact.

In the example, item `I03` got three different levels, one from each panelist:

```{r}
#| label: toy-modal
wide <- data.frame(items[, c("Item_ID", "RP67")], alignments)
r <- sapply(alignments, cor, y = items$RP67)
round(r, 3)
wide$modal <- res_w$modal_items$aligned
wide[3, ]
```

P1 has the highest correlation, so `I03` takes P1's level, Proficient (2). The
correlations are the same ones `emss` reports with each panelist's cut scores:

```{r}
#| label: toy-cor
pan <- extract(res_w, "individual")$panelist
unique(pan[, c("panelist", "correlation")])
```

From here on, $a_i$ is the modal level. In booklet order it is

```{r}
#| label: toy-a
b <- items$RP67
a <- wide$modal
rbind(page = 1:12, RP67 = b, aligned = a)
```

# Step 2: inconsistency of a candidate cut

Take cut level $k$ and a candidate cut score $c$. Item $i$ is
**inconsistent** with $c$ when it lies on the wrong side:

$$
\delta_{ik}(c) =
\underbrace{\mathbf 1[\,a_i \ge k,\; b_i < c\,]}_{\text{upper item below the cut}}
+ \underbrace{\mathbf 1[\,a_i < k,\; b_i \ge c\,]}_{\text{lower item at or above the cut}} .
$$

An item exactly at the cut counts as being in the level the cut opens
(scores at or above $c_k$ are in level $k$). ESS-Count and ESS-Weight are

$$
C_k(c) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \delta_{ik}(c),
\qquad
W_k(c) = \frac{1}{\sigma} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \delta_{ik}(c)\, \lvert b_i - c \rvert .
$$

The figure shows two candidates for the Proficient cut ($k = 2$). Items
aligned Proficient or Advanced are the upper items. Inconsistent items are
drawn filled, with a segment showing their distance to the cut.

```{r}
#| label: fig-candidates
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-cap: "Two candidate Proficient cuts. Filled points are inconsistent items; segments show their distances."
k <- 2
cand <- c(231, 239)
fig <- do.call(rbind, lapply(cand, function(cc) data.frame(
  candidate = sprintf("c = %g", cc), cut = cc, item = items$Item_ID, b = b,
  aligned = factor(labels[a], levels = labels),
  bad = (a >= k & b < cc) | (a < k & b >= cc))))
lab <- aggregate(cbind(count = bad, weight = ifelse(bad, abs(b - cut), 0)) ~ candidate + cut,
                 data = fig, FUN = sum)
ggplot(fig, aes(x = b, y = aligned)) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = cut), linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_segment(data = fig[fig$bad, ], aes(xend = cut, yend = aligned), colour = "#C0392B",
               linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(aes(fill = bad), shape = 21, size = 3, stroke = 0.8) +
  geom_text(aes(label = item), vjust = -1.1, size = 2.6) +
  geom_label(data = lab, aes(x = 300, y = 0.6, label = sprintf("C = %d, W = %g", count, weight)),
             hjust = 1, size = 3.2, inherit.aes = FALSE, label.size = 0) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "white", `TRUE` = "#C0392B"), guide = "none") +
  scale_y_discrete(expand = expansion(add = c(0.8, 0.6))) +
  facet_wrap(~candidate, ncol = 1) +
  labs(x = "RP67", y = "Aligned level") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11)
```

At $c = 231$, two Basic items, `I05` and `I06`, are at or above the cut, at
distances 15 and 21: $C_2 = 2$ and $W_2 = 36$. At $c = 239$, the same two
items are closer (7 and 13), but the Proficient item I03 at 231 is now below
the cut (distance 8): $C_2 = 3$ and $W_2 = 28$. Count prefers 231 and Weight
prefers 239.

# Step 3: the profile and the cut

The **inconsistency profile** evaluates $C_k$ and $W_k$ at every candidate.
`emss` uses the item locations themselves as candidates (the next section
shows that nothing is lost). A direct implementation of the definitions
takes a few lines:

```{r}
#| label: by-hand
ess_by_hand <- function(b, a, k, sd = 1) {
  t(sapply(b, function(c) {
    bad <- (a >= k & b < c) | (a < k & b >= c)
    c(count = sum(bad), weight = sum(abs(b[bad] - c)) / sd)
  }))
}
prof <- data.frame(page = 1:12, RP67 = b, aligned = a,
                   C2 = ess_by_hand(b, a, 2)[, "count"], W2 = ess_by_hand(b, a, 2)[, "weight"],
                   C3 = ess_by_hand(b, a, 3)[, "count"], W3 = ess_by_hand(b, a, 3)[, "weight"])
prof
```

`emss` returns the same profile for the modal alignment:

```{r}
#| label: by-hand-check
emss_prof <- extract(res_w, "profile")[["G5-All"]]
names(emss_prof)
all.equal(unname(as.matrix(prof[, c("C2", "C3", "W2", "W3")])),
          unname(as.matrix(emss_prof[, 4:7])))
```

The cut for level $k$ is the candidate that minimizes the chosen criterion.
Ties are common, so the rule has three parts:

$$
\hat c_k =
\begin{cases}
\text{ESS-Weight:} & \text{minimize } W_k, \text{ then } C_k, \text{ then the page,}\\[2pt]
\text{ESS-Count:} & \text{minimize } C_k, \text{ then } W_k, \text{ then the page,}
\end{cases}
$$

in that order, so the earliest page wins only when both criteria tie. Each
level is minimized separately. Profile values are rounded to 9 decimals
before they are compared. This removes floating-point noise and nothing else,
so the minimum is exact.

The example contains every kind of tie:

* **Proficient, Weight.** $W_2 = 28$ at pages 4 and 5 (a flat stretch of
  the profile). Page 4 has the lower count (3 vs 4), so $\hat c_2 = 239$.
* **Proficient, Count.** $C_2 = 2$ at pages 3 and 7. These pages are not
  adjacent, and page 5 between them has $C_2 = 4$. Page 3 has the lower
  weight (36 vs 46), so $\hat c_2 = 231$.
* **Advanced, Weight.** $W_3 = 0$ at pages 8 and 9. At $c = 265$, item I08
  (Proficient, located at 265) is inconsistent because it sits exactly at
  the cut, but its distance is 0. The count breaks the tie (1 vs 0), so
  $\hat c_3 = 271$. Without the count tie-break, a zero-distance
  inconsistency would go unnoticed.

`plot()` draws the profile of a unit's modal result, with the selected cuts:

```{r}
#| label: fig-profiles
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| fig-cap: "Inconsistency profiles of the modal alignment."
#| fig-subcap:
#|   - "ESS-Weight"
#|   - "ESS-Count"
plot(res_w, "profile", "G5-All")
plot(res_c, "profile", "G5-All")
```

# Properties of the two criteria {#sec-properties}

This section states what the definitions imply. For readability, the proofs
assume distinct item locations. Equal locations change only the bookkeeping
at ties, and every statement was also checked numerically on random data
with tied locations.

Two quantities appear throughout. For the candidate at page $p$, let

$$
u_k(p) = \#\{\, i \in U_k : \text{page}(i) < p \,\}
\quad\text{and}\quad
l_k(p) = \#\{\, i \in L_k : \text{page}(i) \ge p \,\}
$$

be the upper items below the cut and the lower items at or above it. By
definition $C_k(b_{(p)}) = u_k(p) + l_k(p)$.

## Only item locations need to be tried

Between two neighbouring item locations, no item changes side, so:

* $C_k(c)$ is constant on each interval $(b_{(p-1)}, b_{(p)}]$ and on
  $(-\infty, b_{(1)}]$, equal to its value at $b_{(p)}$.
* $W_k(c)$ is linear on each interval $[b_{(p-1)}, b_{(p)}]$ and
  continuous, because an item that crosses the cut is at distance 0 when it
  does.

A linear function on an interval is smallest at one of its ends, so the
minimum of $W_k$ over all $c \le b_{(n)}$ is reached at an item location, and
the same holds for $C_k$. The only cuts not tried are those above the
hardest item, which would leave level $k$ with no items. `emss` therefore
always places a cut on an item, and the cut item's page is reported with it.

## ESS-Count is a walk through the booklet

Moving the candidate from page $p$ to page $p+1$ moves exactly one item, the
item on page $p$, from the "at or above" side to the "below" side. If that
item is an upper item, it becomes inconsistent; if it is a lower item, it
stops being inconsistent:

$$
C_k(b_{(p+1)}) - C_k(b_{(p)}) =
\begin{cases} +1 & a_{(p)} \ge k,\\ -1 & a_{(p)} < k, \end{cases}
\qquad C_k(b_{(1)}) = n_{<k}.
$$

So the Count profile is a walk that starts at the number of lower items and
steps up for every upper item and down for every lower item in booklet
order. ESS-Count puts the cut where the walk is lowest. The walk can come
back to the same low value several times, which is why Count ties are
common and need not be adjacent. Here is the Proficient walk in the example:

```{r}
#| label: walk
steps <- ifelse(a >= 2, +1, -1)
walk <- sum(a < 2) + c(0, cumsum(steps))[1:12]
rbind(page = 1:12, aligned = a, step = steps, C2 = walk)
identical(walk, prof$C2)
```

The walk depends only on the order of the aligned levels in the booklet.
The distances between items never enter it.

## ESS-Weight is a quantile of the item locations {#sec-quantile}

Write $\sigma W_k(c) = \sum_{i \in U_k} (c - b_i)_+ + \sum_{i \in L_k} (b_i - c)_+$,
where $(x)_+ = \max(x, 0)$. Between neighbouring locations, the derivative
with respect to $c$ is

$$
\sigma \frac{d W_k}{d c}
= \#\{ i \in U_k : b_i < c \} - \#\{ i \in L_k : b_i > c \}
= \underbrace{\#\{ i : b_i < c \}}_{\text{items below the cut}} - \; n_{<k},
$$

because the lower items above the cut are all lower items minus those below
it. Above page $p$ there are $p$ items below the cut, so the slope between
pages $p$ and $p+1$ is $(p - n_{<k}) / \sigma$:

$$
W_k(b_{(p+1)}) - W_k(b_{(p)}) = \frac{(p - n_{<k}) \,\big(b_{(p+1)} - b_{(p)}\big)}{\sigma}.
$$

The slope is negative before page $n_{<k}$, zero between pages $n_{<k}$ and
$n_{<k}+1$, and positive after. This has three consequences:

1. $W_k$ is **convex**, and its minimum is reached at pages $n_{<k}$ and
   $n_{<k} + 1$, with equal values.
2. The **ESS-Weight cut** for level $k$ is the location of the item on page
   $n_{<k}$ or page $n_{<k} + 1$. The count breaks the tie: it is page
   $n_{<k}$ if that item is aligned at or above $k$ and page $n_{<k} + 1$
   otherwise (from the walk in the previous section).
3. *Which* items are aligned below level $k$ does not matter, only *how
   many*. The alignment pattern decides only between the two neighbouring
   items. ESS-Weight places the cut so that the number of items below it
   matches the number of items aligned below the level. It is the same
   property that makes the median minimize the total absolute distance.

In the example, $n_{<2} = 4$ and $n_{<3} = 8$. The minima of $W_2$ are at
pages 4 and 5 and those of $W_3$ at pages 8 and 9. Item I04 on page 4 is
aligned Proficient ($\ge 2$), so $\hat c_2$ is on page 4. Item I08 on page 8 is
aligned Proficient ($< 3$), so $\hat c_3$ is on page 9:

```{r}
#| label: quantile-check
n_below <- c(Proficient = sum(a < 2), Advanced = sum(a < 3))
n_below
res_w$modal[res_w$modal$table == "All", c("level", "page", "cut_score")]
```

The minimal weight itself still reflects the pattern: it is the total
distance of the inconsistent items, here 28 for Proficient and 0 for
Advanced. What the pattern cannot do is move the Weight cut by more than one
item.

## Location scale and SD

Both properties above depend only on the **order** of the items, not on the
distances between them. Hence:

* For any strictly increasing transformation $g$ of the location scale (for
  example theta to scale scores, or a nonlinear scale conversion), the
  ESS-Weight cut is on the same item, and the cut score is $g(\hat c_k)$.
* The Count profile is unchanged by $g$. The ESS-Count cut can change only
  when there is a Count tie, because the tie is broken by the weight, which
  does use distances.
* A change of location that reorders items can move both cuts. For example,
  RP50 and RP67 locations from a 2PL or 3PL model order items differently
  when item discriminations differ. Under the Rasch model, every RP value
  shifts all items equally, so the cuts are on the same items.
* Dividing by the SD $\sigma$ rescales every weight by the same factor. It
  changes the reported weights, which then are in SD units and comparable
  across grades, but never the cut scores.

```{r}
#| label: scale-check
d_theta <- d
d_theta$items$theta <- (d$items$RP67 - 250) / 30        # a linear scale change
d_theta$items$expo  <- exp(d_theta$items$theta)         # a nonlinear, increasing one
sapply(c("RP67", "theta", "expo"), function(loc) {
  m <- emstans(data = d_theta, location = loc)$modal
  m$page[m$table == "All"]
})
```

The pages of the two all-tables cuts are the same on all three scales.

## Cut scores are always in order

The cut for each level is found separately, yet the cuts never cross:
$\hat c_2 \le \hat c_3 \le \dots \le \hat c_K$.

* **ESS-Weight.** $n_{<k}$ increases with $k$, so the candidate pages
  $\{n_{<k}, n_{<k}+1\}$ move up with $k$. When $n_{<k} = n_{<k+1}$ (no item
  is aligned to level $k$), the two profiles are identical, the two cuts
  fall on the same item, and level $k$ is empty.
* **ESS-Count.** Going from level $k$ to $k+1$ moves the items aligned to
  level $k$ from the upper to the lower group. This adds the term
  $\#\{a_i = k, b_i \ge c\} - \#\{a_i = k, b_i < c\}$ to the Count and
  $\sum_{a_i = k} (b_i - c)/\sigma$ to the Weight, and both are
  nonincreasing in $c$. Suppose $\hat c_{k+1} < \hat c_k$. Because the added
  terms are nonincreasing, $\hat c_{k+1}$ can only win if it already tied
  with $\hat c_k$ on $C_k$, and then the tie-break that selected $\hat c_k$
  means $W_k(\hat c_k) < W_k(\hat c_{k+1})$. That inequality survives the
  added Weight term, so $\hat c_k$ would also beat $\hat c_{k+1}$ for level
  $k+1$, a contradiction. The weight tie-break is what guarantees this.

Smoothed cut scores (`smooth = TRUE`, below) are not covered by these
arguments.

## What the minimum values add up to {#sec-totals}

Because the cuts are ordered, an item's empirical level satisfies
$o_i \ge k \iff b_i \ge \hat c_k$, so item $i$ is inconsistent with exactly
$\lvert a_i - o_i \rvert$ of the cuts (the cuts between its aligned and its
empirical level). Summing over levels:

$$
\sum_{k=2}^{K} C_k(\hat c_k) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \lvert a_i - o_i \rvert,
\qquad
\sum_{k=2}^{K} W_k(\hat c_k) = \frac{1}{\sigma} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \sum_{k \text{ between } o_i \text{ and } a_i} \lvert b_i - \hat c_k \rvert .
$$

Since the separate minima are ordered, they also minimize these sums over
all ordered sets of cuts. **ESS-Count chooses the cut scores that minimize
the total level disagreement $\sum_i \lvert a_i - o_i \rvert$** between
aligned and empirical levels. ESS-Weight minimizes the total distance from
each misplaced item to every cut it is on the wrong side of.

```{r}
#| label: totals-check
mc <- res_c$modal[res_c$modal$table == "All", ]
sum(mc$count)
mi <- res_c$modal_items
sum(abs(mi$aligned - mi$operational))
```

## Count or Weight?

| | ESS-Count | ESS-Weight |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Minimizes | number of misplaced items; across levels, total level disagreement | total distance of misplaced items from the cut |
| Profile | a walk, with possibly several separated minima | convex, minimum at pages $n_{<k}$ and $n_{<k}+1$ |
| Depends on | the order of aligned levels in the booklet | the number of items aligned below each level; the pattern only picks between two neighbouring items |
| Ties | frequent (integer values), broken by the weight | at most two neighbouring items, broken by the count |
| Location scale | order only, except weight tie-breaks | order only |

ESS-Weight is the default in `emss`. Its cuts are stable: changing one item's
alignment changes $n_{<k}$ by at most one, so it moves a cut by at most two
pages. ESS-Count responds to *where*
the misaligned items are, so it is the criterion to look at when the
question is which items the panelists placed out of order. Reporting both is
cheap, and large differences between them are worth a look at the item
review.

# From cut scores to the other results

## Empirical levels

Given the cuts, the **empirical** (operational) level of an item is the
level its location falls in:

$$
o_i = 1 + \#\{\, k : \hat c_k \le b_i \,\}.
$$

An item exactly at a cut belongs to the level the cut opens. If two cuts
fall on the same item, the level between them is empty and items at that
location go to the higher level.

## Agreement

The crosstab of empirical by aligned level, with entries $n_{\ell m}$ (items
with $o_i = \ell$ and $a_i = m$), gives:

* exact agreement $\sum_\ell n_{\ell\ell} / n$, adjacent disagreements
  ($\lvert a_i - o_i \rvert = 1$) and discrepant ones ($\ge 2$);
* the weighted kappa (Cohen, 1968) with quadratic weights, as computed by
  `psych::cohen.kappa()`:

$$
\kappa_w = 1 - \frac{\sum_{\ell,m} (\ell - m)^2\, n_{\ell m}}
{\sum_{\ell,m} (\ell - m)^2\, n_{\ell \cdot}\, n_{\cdot m} / n}.
$$

```{r}
#| label: agreement
ag <- extract(res_w, "detailed")
ag$agreement
ct <- xtabs(n ~ operational + aligned, ag$crosstab[ag$crosstab$type == "exact", ])
ct
w <- outer(1:3, 1:3, function(l, m) (l - m)^2)
1 - sum(w * ct) / sum(w * outer(rowSums(ct), colSums(ct)) / sum(ct))
```

## Item review

For each inconsistent item, the item review reports a signed distance from
the cut that bounds its aligned level. Writing $\hat c_{K+1} = +\infty$:

$$
d_i =
\begin{cases}
b_i - \hat c_{a_i} & a_i > o_i \quad\text{(located below its aligned level; } d_i < 0\text{)},\\[2pt]
b_i - (\hat c_{a_i + 1} - 1) & a_i < o_i \quad\text{(located above its aligned level; } d_i > 0\text{)},\\[2pt]
0 & a_i = o_i .
\end{cases}
$$

The "$-1$" treats the top of a level as one score point below the next cut,
as on an integer scale-score metric. On a continuous metric such as theta it
adds one unit to the distance of items located too high. The review also
reports $\lvert d_i \rvert / \sigma$.

```{r}
#| label: review
rv <- extract(res_w, "review")
rv[rv$status != "Consistent", c("item_id", "page", "aligned", "operational", "location",
                                "distance", "status")]
```

Item I05 is 7 points above the Proficient cut (its contribution to $W_2$),
and its review distance is $246 - (239 - 1) = 8$.

## Essential consistency

A small misplacement may not be worth flagging. With an **essential consistency** margin $\mathrm{EC}$ on the location scale (the setup's EC
column, or `ess_data(ec = )`):

* the item review labels an inconsistent item *Essentially Consistent* when
  $0 < \lvert d_i \rvert \le \mathrm{EC}$ and *Inconsistent* when
  $\lvert d_i \rvert > \mathrm{EC}$;
* the EC-adjusted crosstab (type `"ec"`) treats items with
  $\lvert d_i \rvert < \mathrm{EC}$ as agreeing, setting their aligned level
  to their empirical level.

An item exactly at the margin counts as essentially consistent in the review
but not in the crosstab. EC never changes the cut scores. With `EC = 10` in the
example, `I03` and `I05` are within the margin and `I06` is not:

```{r}
#| label: ec
res_ec <- emstans(data = ess_data(ratings, items, levels = labels, ec = 10), location = "RP67")
extract(res_ec, "review")[c(3, 5, 6), c("item_id", "distance", "status")]
extract(res_ec, "detailed")$agreement
```

## Panelist, median and average cuts

Every panelist's own alignments go through Steps 2 and 3, giving panelist
cuts $\hat c_{jk}$ with their pages. For each table and for all tables, `emss`
reports two summaries of them. The **median** cut is the cut score at the
middle page (the mean of the two middle panelists' cut scores when $J$ is
even), which equals the median of the panelist cut scores. The **average**
cut is $\bar c_k = \frac1J \sum_j \hat c_{jk}$, and its page is that of the
panelist whose cut is closest to it.

```{r}
#| label: panelists
pan[, c("panelist", "cut_level", "page", "cut_score", "count", "weight")]
ind <- extract(res_w, "individual")
rbind(median  = ind$median$cut_score[ind$median$table == "All"],
      average = ind$average$cut_score[ind$average$table == "All"])
```

The modal cut and the summaries of panelist cuts answer different questions.
The modal cut is the best cut for the group's consensus alignment. The
median and average describe the spread of individual judgements.

## Impact

With examinee score frequencies $f_s$ ($N = \sum_s f_s$), the percentage of
examinees in level $k$, at or above it, and below it are

$$
\text{in}_k = \frac{100}{N} \sum_{\hat c_k \le s < \hat c_{k+1}} f_s,
\qquad
\text{at or above}_k = \frac{100}{N} \sum_{s \ge \hat c_k} f_s,
\qquad
\text{below}_k = \frac{100}{N} \sum_{s < \hat c_k} f_s,
$$

with $\hat c_1 = -\infty$ and $\hat c_{K+1} = +\infty$. The impact table also
gives each level's pages in the ordered item booklet: level $k$ runs from
the page of $\hat c_k$ to the page before $\hat c_{k+1}$.

```{r}
#| label: impact
extract(res_w, "summary")
```

## Analysis units {#sec-units}

Everything above is computed per unit: grade × round × item subset.

* **Grades** are always analysed separately, each with its own levels, SD
  and EC.
* **Rounds:** when the ratings contain several rounds, each round is a
  separate unit, for example `G5-All Round 2`.
* **Domains:** with `by_domain = TRUE`, each content domain is also analysed
  on its own items, in addition to all items (`G5-Algebra`, ...).

# Smoothed cut scores

With `smooth = TRUE`, each profile column is smoothed before the minimum is
taken. A Gaussian GAM, $y = f(b) + \varepsilon$, with a penalized regression
spline $f$ (`mgcv::gam(y ~ s(b, k = q))`, $q = 10$ basis functions when
$n > 20$, otherwise $n/2$) is fitted to the profile values at the item
locations. The cut is the minimizer of $\hat f$ over 200 equally spaced
points across the location range (rounded to 2 decimals), and its page is
the first item at or above it. Smoothed cuts need not be item locations, and
the ordering guarantee above does not apply to them.

# How emss computes the profiles

Evaluating the definitions directly costs $O(n^2)$ per level: $n$
candidates, each checked against $n$ items. `emss` sorts the upper and lower
locations once and keeps their cumulative sums $S_U$ and $S_L$. For a
candidate $c$, a binary search gives $u = \#\{U: b < c\}$ and
$\lambda = \#\{L: b < c\}$, and then

$$
C_k(c) = u + (n_L - \lambda),
\qquad
\sigma W_k(c) = \big(c\,u - S_U(u)\big) + \big(S_L(n_L) - S_L(\lambda) - c\,(n_L - \lambda)\big),
$$

with $n_L = n_{<k}$. All candidates together cost $O(n \log n)$. The test
suite checks this against the direct definition (`ess_by_hand()` above is
the same check in miniature).
